transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-11
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel, Miguel Santos (Redwood); Ravi Menon, Leah Kim, Omar Velez (Sparrow AI)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): SE walked through runtime trace samples, KV cache hit pattern, impact of hotkeys, and differences between streaming non-streaming token emission on p95/p99 tail. Customer provided network topology and highlighted an intermittent 60-200ms tail they see in production on multi-region requests.

Topics: p95/p99 measurement methodology; streaming vs non-streaming tail behavior; KV cache hotkeys and prefix locality; batching and quantization tradeoffs; VPC network hops and overlay latency.

Action items (from transcript): Miguel to run KV hotspot test; Omar to send traceroute and subnet map; Leah to provide prompt corpus.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Aisha Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros?
[00:10] Ravi Menon: ravi here, cto at sparrow ai. we build the question-answering layer for the customer support use case.
[00:15] Leah Kim: leah, head of ml eng — focused on inference infra and cost.
[00:20] Omar Velez: omar, infra eng, i own VPC/networking and k8s overlay.
[00:26] Miguel Santos: miguel from redwood runtime, i looked at the traces you sent. there's a few patterns i want to call out, especially around kv cache eviction and network path length.
[00:35] Leah Kim: cool. our symptom: production p99 for short completions (<=40 tokens) spikes to 600-900ms intermittently; p95 around 220-260ms baseline. streaming seems to help sometimes but not consistently.
[00:50] Miguel Santos: ok, that's helpful. when you say streaming helps, do you mean you see earlier bytes and the client is happy, or the server-side tail actually improves?
[00:58] Leah Kim: client appears happier because first token arrives earlier; but server side p99 measured at server still has those spikes — so there is ambiguity in observability.
[01:10] Aisha Patel: right, we often see that UX masks server-side tail if you stream first token quickly. but for other operations you need actual p99.
[01:18] Ravi Menon: we provided traces — i don't know all the names in the trace, but you saw the multi-hop? we have traffic going to the inference plane through a proxy in another AZ for egress control.
[01:30] Omar Velez: yes there's a two-hop path: app pod -> proxy (nginx) -> model service node. cross-AZ sometimes.
[01:37] Miguel Santos: two hops can absolutely add variance. small adds: normal single-hop adds ~10-20ms; cross-AZ jump and proxy cost adds jitter. but the bigger issue i flagged is the kv cache "hotkey" behavior — when many requests share the same prefix, one node gets high cache locality and eviction churn.
[01:58] Leah Kim: we've been using prefix-based caching in our proxy — so that makes sense. what specifically is happening with eviction?
[02:06] Miguel Santos: in the traces you sent, the node that's primary for that kv set did a lot of disk-backed fallback lookups — not in-memory — either because of cache pressure or quantization memory layout. that's why you sometimes see a long tail ~300-800ms.
[02:22] Omar Velez: hmm, we use small instance types for cost reasons on that AZ. could that be causing the node to swap or GC and evict items?
[02:30] Miguel Santos: yep, memory pressure and non-optimal shard placement will cause eviction. also if your batching is small and you set continuous batching low, the runtime may flush kv to disk for longer contexts.
[02:42] Leah Kim: when you say "continuous batching low" — do you mean the batching windows? we run micro-batches of 8, often 40ms windows.
[02:51] Miguel Santos: micro-batch 8 at 40ms is okay, but for prefix-heavy workloads it can starve the upstream of batching benefits. you might see more random network IO if the batch doesn't aggregate key lookups.
[03:03] Ravi Menon: can you explain streaming vs non-streaming in this context? i.e., how does streaming affect kv cache and p99?
[03:10] Miguel Santos: good question. streaming (server-sent token emission) helps perceived latency, because you can emit tokens while the model continues compute. however, the server still needs to do kv cache lookups and kv cache population for the ongoing decoding steps. in some implementations, streaming enables earlier flushes of the kv cache into the pipeline which can increase memory churn. that said, streaming itself doesn't magically fix backend p99 — it just exposes earlier bytes.
[03:38] Leah Kim: so i think we've conflated two measurements: client-experienced TTF (time to first token) and server-side p99 for completion. we need separate telemetry for both.
[03:48] Aisha Patel: yes, separate metrics. redwood recommends instrumenting both: time-to-first-byte at the edge and end-to-end server invocation p95/p99 measured at the model runtime.
[04:00] Omar Velez: we can add a server-side tag in our tracing, that won't be hard. i'll try to push that change this week.
[04:06] Miguel Santos: perfect. also in the traces i saw a couple of requests that hit a distant AZ because of routing policy during autoscale. that increases p99. any cross-AZ routing heuristics?
[04:18] Omar Velez: autoscale scheduler occasionally spins up nodes in a cold AZ; loadbalancer then spreads traffic. we haven't pinned model shards to AZs.
[04:26] Miguel Santos: for tail-sensitive workloads you want AZ affinity or sticky routing for a fraction of traffic. otherwise cold nodes will pay startup jitter and warm-up effects, plus cold cache.
[04:36] Leah Kim: is pinning shards supported on redwood private? we were thinking about dedicated to avoid noisy neighbors.
[04:43] Miguel Santos: yes, Dedicated and Private allow you to pin capacity and set allocation policies. but still shard placement matters — we'll recommend pinning hot prefixes to a stable shard set.
[04:55] Ravi Menon: ok, are there quantization concerns too? we shipped an 8-bit quantized model recently. could quantization amplify tail?
[05:02] Miguel Santos: quantization changes memory layout and compute kernel selection. in some runtimes, 8-bit kernels are faster but use different buffer management; if kernel fallback happens (e.g., unsupported op), that can cause spikes. also reduced memory headroom can increase eviction. so yes, it's plausible quantization contributed.
[05:21] Leah Kim: do you have recommended quant profiles? we are using a blanket 8-bit config.
[05:26] Miguel Santos: we'll share our quantization doc — generally for high-throughput short-completion workloads, 8-bit asymmetric with per-channel scales tends to be good; but validate with your prompt mix. some customers prefer 4-bit for cost but accept more tail variance.
[05:40] Aisha Patel: we'll attach the quantization guide to the follow-up email.
[05:44] Omar Velez: coming back to networking — traceroutes in the packet capture show a NAT box in front of the inference node; that's where we sometimes observe extra 30-80ms.
[05:55] Miguel Santos: NAT plus proxy plus cross-AZ hops is additive. when measuring p99, attribute per-hop latency and variance. also measure queuing delays at the proxy.
[06:05] Ravi Menon: how do you recommend we partition traffic to measure reliably? we don't want to bias results by only hitting caches.
[06:12] Miguel Santos: design a two-phase microbench: 1) cold-start series — spin up nodes and hammer with unique prefixes to measure cold p99; 2) hot-path series — use your typical prefix distribution and run steady-state to measure cache effects. that's how we isolate cold vs hot tails.
[06:28] Leah Kim: sounds good. what's the recommended sample size?
[06:31] Miguel Santos: for p99 you need thousands of samples per configuration; for quick runs, 5k-10k is good. keep a representative traffic mix (we can help build the corpus).
[06:42] Aisha Patel: also collect kernel-level logs if possible — the runtime produces slow-path counters when it falls back to disk or a slower kernel.
[06:50] Omar Velez: is that an option in private deployment?
[06:53] Miguel Santos: yes — Private and Dedicated expose extra diagnostics. hosted plan has less low-level visibility but we can enable extended logs for pilot customers.
[07:02] Ravi Menon: we want to run a test that reproduces the 700-900ms spikes. any test config recommendations?
[07:09] Miguel Santos: try: 1) single-node test with heavy prefix collision (simulate hotkey), 2) multi-node two-hop test with NAT/proxy, 3) quantized vs fp16 run. For each, run 10k requests and report p50/p95/p99 and cpu/gpu mem usage and kernel-fallback counters.
[07:27] Leah Kim: we'll assemble that. will you provide scripts?
[07:30] Miguel Santos: yes we'll share our microbench harness and a template for the csv/spreadsheet.
[07:35] Aisha Patel: quick clarification — when comparing streaming vs non-streaming, it's important to hold batch config constant. otherwise you're measuring two variables.
[07:44] Leah Kim: makes sense. we'll hold batch size and continuous-batch windows constant.
[07:48] Omar Velez: on the routing note, is there a recommended network topology for private deploys? we currently use an overlay that spans AZs for resilience.
[07:57] Miguel Santos: overlay is fine but for ultra-low tail you want at least two things: 1) localized inference nodes (AZ affinity) for hot routes; 2) lightweight ingress (avoid proxy layers if you can control egress). also use tcp tuning — keepalive and larger recv buffers to reduce jitter.
[08:13] Ravi Menon: any quick wins for immediate improvement?
[08:16] Miguel Santos: a few quick wins: 1) enable sticky routing for 10% of traffic to warm nodes; 2) increase kv cache size for hot prefixes; 3) temporarily allocate a larger instance type in that AZ to avoid swap; 4) set kernel fallback logging to verbose for one day to identify slow-path ops.
[08:32] Leah Kim: can we temporarily bump instance size without too much cost? yes we can, ok we'll try that in staging first.
[08:38] Miguel Santos: on batching — you mentioned 40ms windows; experiment with 80ms for long-tail improvements. it increases average token latency slightly but can reduce p99 by improving batch aggregation and reducing per-request overhead.
[08:50] Aisha Patel: remember to measure cost delta vs tail improvement. that's part of Redwood Optimize's recommendations.
[08:56] Ravi Menon: do you have tooling to simulate hotspot prefixes?
[08:59] Miguel Santos: yes our harness supports synthetic key distributions — zipfian and hotkey. we'll share the config.
[09:06] Omar Velez: i'll send the traceroute and VPC mapping after the call; any specific format?
[09:10] Miguel Santos: plain text is fine, include timestamps and which AZ the hop corresponds to.
[09:15] Leah Kim: on quantization, if we see kernel fallback, is it usually a driver or runtime bug?
[09:21] Miguel Santos: often it's a mismatch: model ops compiled for one kernel layout but runtime selects a fallback due to sequence length or an unsupported op. we'll correlate the fallback counters to the op graph.
[09:33] Ravi Menon: what's the expected lead time to get meaningful numbers from your microbench?
[09:36] Miguel Santos: we'll turn around initial results in 2-3 business days after we get access to a dev cluster and prompt corpus.
[09:43] Aisha Patel: ok, let's recap next steps before we wrap.
[09:47] Miguel Santos: recap: miguel will provision a small dedicated cluster and run three microbench scenarios; omar will send traceroute + vpc info; leah will supply prompt corpus; aisha will send quant guide and the microbench harness link. we'll aim to have initial results by 2026-02-18.
[10:06] Ravi Menon: great. thanks, everyone. any final questions?
[10:10] Leah Kim: one more — do you recommend changing our proxy config concurrently with tests? could we flip sticky routing on during test window?
[10:17] Miguel Santos: yes, flip sticky routing for a controlled fraction (10-20%) to validate its impact. keep detailed logs so we can compare tails.
[10:26] Omar Velez: noted. i'll schedule the routing change in a maintenance window.
[10:30] Aisha Patel: i'll send meeting notes and attach the quant doc and harness links. thanks all.
[10:36] Miguel Santos: thanks, bye.
[10:40] (call ends)
